plan: In a second-price (Vickrey) auction, bidding one's true value is a dominant strategy regardless of what other rational bidders do. This is because I pay the second-highest bid if I win, not my own bid, so overbidding risks paying more than my value, and underbidding risks losing profitable wins. Since my value is $40, I should bid exactly $40 to maximize expected profit.

In a second-price sealed-bid auction, bidding your true value is a dominant strategy regardless of the number of competitors or their strategies. This is because you pay the second-highest bid if you win, not your own bid, so bidding truthfully maximizes expected profit: you win whenever your value exceeds the second-highest bid (profitable), and lose otherwise (correctly avoiding unprofitable wins). With my value at $13, I should bid exactly $13 to ensure optimal outcomes.

This is a second-price sealed-bid auction with 3 bidders and uniform values on [0,49]. The optimal strategy (Nash equilibrium) in this setting is to bid a fraction of my true value, specifically bid = value * (n-1)/n = value * 2/3, since truthful bidding isn't optimal in second-price auctions with common priors when bidders shade bids strategically... actually in second-price auctions, truthful bidding IS the dominant strategy regardless of others' behavior. I should bid my true value of $17.
